stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the record of the Sacco and Vanzetti case: In 1920, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, two Italian immigrants and anarchists, were arrested in Massachusetts and charged with robbing a shoe-factory payroll and killing two men. They were convicted in 1921. Many observers questioned whether the trial had been fair, pointing to the judge's conduct and the men's radical politics. After six years of appeals, both men were executed in August 1927.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the case record as summarized in 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 22.

rationales.A: Protests on two continents are the opposite of a local dispute. The case was watched around the world.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the seven-year case drew international attention because it raised the question of whether America tried immigrants fairly. Abroad, the two men stood for that question itself.
rationales.C: Worldwide protests argued the trial had been unfair. Protests are evidence of doubt, not of fairness.
rationales.D: The protests drew writers, workers, and ordinary citizens abroad. Support reached far beyond anarchist circles.
rationales.general:
1. Ask where the protests happened: in cities in Europe and Latin America.
2. Ask what people abroad were protesting: an American trial, not their own laws.
3. Ask why they cared: the case raised a question about American justice itself.
4. Name what the case had become: a symbol, debated far beyond Massachusetts.
Remember: when a local case draws protests abroad, it has stopped being only about its own facts.
